407.title: Eat, drink, don't waste
407.hook: eat and drink but don't be wasteful (7:31)
407.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to avoid israf in food, water and money; some keep the hadith of thirds in mind at meals, and teachers often point to the small amount of water the Prophet used for wudu.

segments.voice: Yesterday: libas, the garment, and the garment of piety. Your line was the best clothing is inside. What did you put on? Today, five verses later, from the closet to the kitchen. Day four hundred seven.

Open almost any fridge on a Sunday night. Half a bag of spinach gone slimy. The leftover rice nobody wanted. A yogurt two weeks past its date. Food that was paid for goes in the bin, and more gets bought. At the other end of the scale, a hadith shows the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ washing for prayer with about a double handful of water. Between those two pictures sits a short line in surah seven, five verses after the garment of piety, that sounds almost too simple to need saying.
screen: `THE SUNDAY NIGHT FRIDGE.` → `A DOUBLE HANDFUL OF WATER.` → `TOO SIMPLE TO NEED SAYING.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “O Children of Adam! Look to your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals.” Two halves. The first is about clothing again. A report in Sahih Muslim explains why: before Islam, some people circled the Ka'bah unclothed, and this verse told them to come to worship dressed, even dressed well. The second half is about the table. Eat. Drink. Enjoy it; the next verse asks who could forbid the good things Allah has provided. But don't commit israf. The root s-r-f means to go past the limit, to overshoot. Israf is excess: too much, beyond what's needed. The Qur'an has a separate word, tabdhir, in surah seventeen, for scattering wealth away on nothing, and it's sharp about both. A hadith in Tirmidhi's collection gives a measure for eating: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath. And Bukhari records that the Prophet made wudu with a mudd, roughly what two cupped hands can hold, and bathed with only a few times that. Teachers take it as a lesson: enough is a real amount, and you can find it. Notice the verse doesn't say eat less than you need, or never enjoy food. It says eat, drink, and stop at enough. The opposite of israf isn't hunger. It's the right amount, used well.
screen: `DRESSED FOR WORSHIP.` · `EAT AND DRINK — ENJOY IT.` · `ISRAF — PAST THE LIMIT.` · `A THIRD, A THIRD, A THIRD.` · then, large: `BE NOT PRODIGAL.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Walk through your day ahead in your mind and look for the leaks: water left running while you brush your teeth, food that will go bad, a light left on in an empty room, a purchase you don't need. Don't judge. Just notice. Pick one leak and plan to close it today. And at your next meal, try to stop at enough, with a little room left for breath. The bell holds the time.
Israf. Excess, going past the limit. Surah seven: eat and drink, but don't be wasteful, for Allah does not love the wasteful. Today's word.
Your line: enough, no waste. Today, waste nothing you can save: one meal finished, one tap turned off, one thing not bought. Day four hundred seven.

fork.reveal: a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath (Tirmidhi). enough is the goal, not hunger.

original.note: Arabic: excess, extravagance, from s-r-f, to go past the limit.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't waste food.
what it means: enjoy what's provided, dressed with dignity, and stop at enough in food, drink and everything else.
what a scholar hears: israf (excess in quantity) and tabdhir (spending on what has no right) are distinct terms; Muslim 3028 gives the occasion of 7:31 as unclothed circling of the Ka'bah.

408.title: Humbly and in secret
408.hook: call on your Lord humbly and privately, with fear and hope (7:55–56)
408.howItsDone: Muslims make du'a, personal supplication, at any time and in any language, often quietly after the prayer or in prostration; teachers cite 7:55 for keeping it humble and low-voiced.

segments.voice: Yesterday: israf, going past the limit. Your line was enough, no waste. Did one leak get closed? Today, a limit of another kind: how loud to be when you call on God. Day four hundred eight.

On a journey with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, his companions climbed a hill and, the way travelers do, shouted Allahu akbar into the valley at the top of their lungs. A report in Bukhari says he turned to them and told them, gently, to take it easy on themselves. You're not calling someone deaf, he said, or someone far away. You're calling one who hears, and who is near. Grown men, mid-shout, lowering their voices. Surah seven, verse fifty-five, says the same thing as a command.
screen: `SHOUTING INTO THE VALLEY.` → `NOT DEAF, NOT FAR AWAY.` → `ONE WHO HEARS, AND IS NEAR.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “Call upon your Lord humbly and in secret. Lo! He loveth not aggressors.” Two Arabic words carry the manner. Tadarru'an: humbly, with the kind of pleading a person does when they really need something. And khufyatan: hidden, privately, under your breath. The prophet Zakariyya does exactly this in surah nineteen: he calls his Lord in a secret call, an old man asking quietly for a child. The verse then warns that Allah doesn't love those who overstep. Commentators gave examples of overstepping in du'a: shouting, praying for something harmful, or demanding absurd detail. A report in Abu Dawud's collection tells of a companion who heard his son ask for the white palace on the right side of paradise, and told him to ask simply for paradise. The next verse adds two more words: call on Him in fear and hope, khawfan wa tama'an. Not only fear, which can crush. Not only hope, which can turn careless. Both, like two wings of a bird, as some scholars put it. And the verse ends: the mercy of Allah is near to those who do good. Notice the word near, the same thing the Prophet said on the hill. In this teaching, a quiet du'a doesn't need an audience, a microphone, or perfect Arabic. It can happen at a red light, in the shower, at two in the morning. The verse asks only that it be humble, and that it be yours.
screen: `TADARRU' — HUMBLY, PLEADING.` · `KHUFYAH — HIDDEN, UNDER THE BREATH.` · `DON'T OVERSTEP.` · `FEAR AND HOPE, TWO WINGS.` · then, large: `HUMBLY AND IN SECRET.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your voice go quiet, even inside your head. Think of one thing you actually need, plainly: health for someone, a way through a problem, a softer heart. If you pray, you can make a du'a for it now, in your own words, under your breath, with no one to hear but the One you're asking. If you don't pray, simply hold that need quietly, with both a little fear and a little hope. The bell holds the time.
Tadarru'an, humbly, the way someone pleads when they truly need something. Call on your Lord that way, and in secret, in fear and hope, for His mercy is near. Today's word.
Your line: humbly, in secret. Today, find one private moment, a red light, a hallway, and use it for one quiet ask. Day four hundred eight.

409.title: Hud and 'Ad
409.hook: Hud warns the builders of high towers, and the wind comes (7:65–72)
409.howItsDone: Muslims honor Hud as a prophet sent to the Arabian people of 'Ad; surah eleven bears his name, and teachers read his story as a warning against trusting strength and wealth instead of God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tadarru'an, humbly and in secret. Your line was humbly, in secret. Did you find a quiet moment for one ask? Today surah seven begins a run of prophets, one people at a time. Day four hundred nine.

Cities race each other for the tallest building, and boast when they win. Glass towers, stone walls, a bigger house, a bigger bank balance, a big following. Building isn't wrong. But sometimes people build not to shelter anyone, only to feel that nothing can touch them. The Qur'an tells of an ancient Arabian people called 'Ad, famous for their strength and their building, and of a man from among them sent to warn them. His name was Hud.
screen: `EVERY AGE HAS ITS TALLEST BUILDING.` → `BUILT TO FEEL UNTOUCHABLE.` → `A PEOPLE CALLED 'AD.`

segments.voice: Surah seven, verse sixty-five, introduces him simply: to 'Ad, their brother Hud. Not a stranger. One of their own. His message is the one Nuh brought just before him: my people, worship Allah, you have no god but Him. He reminds them that Allah made them successors after the people of Nuh and gave them great stature and strength. The chiefs answer that he's a fool and a liar, and they say they will not leave what their fathers worshipped. The story is told in several surahs, and they fill in the picture. In surah twenty-six, Hud asks them: do you build a landmark on every high place, just for show, and fortresses, as if you'll live forever? In surah forty-one, they boast: who is mightier than us in strength? Surah eighty-nine names their city Iram, of the lofty pillars. Then the end. Surah forty-six says they saw a cloud coming toward their valleys and said, this cloud will bring us rain. It wasn't rain. Surah sixty-nine calls it a furious, roaring wind, sent against them for seven nights and eight days, until they lay like the hollow trunks of palm trees. Surah seven says simply that Allah saved Hud and those with him, and cut off the rest. Where were they? Surah forty-six places them at al-Ahqaf, the sand dunes, which commentators set in southern Arabia. More than that, the sources don't say for certain. The lesson doesn't need the map. Towers, pillars, strength: none of it was safety.
screen: `THEIR BROTHER HUD.` · `A LANDMARK ON EVERY HIGH PLACE.` · `A CLOUD THEY THOUGHT WAS RAIN.` · `SEVEN NIGHTS, EIGHT DAYS.` · then, large: `TOWERS AREN'T SAFETY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly: what do I build to feel strong? Savings, a title, a reputation, a body at the gym, the number of people who'd take my side. None of these is bad. Pick one, and hold it in your mind. Then ask: if it were gone tomorrow, what would still hold me up? Stay with whatever answer comes, even if it's quiet. The bell holds the time.
Hud. A prophet sent to his own people, the great builders of ancient Arabia, 'Ad, who trusted their strength until the wind came. Today's word.
Your line: towers aren't safety. Today, when you reach for the thing that makes you feel strong, notice it, and remember the wind. Day four hundred nine.

410.title: Salih and the she-camel
410.hook: Thamud are given a she-camel as a sign and told to let her graze (7:73–79)
410.howItsDone: Muslims honor Salih as a prophet sent to Thamud; his story is taught alongside hadith on kindness to animals, and teachers recall the reports about the Prophet passing al-Hijr.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hud and 'Ad, and the wind. Your line was towers aren't safety. What did you notice yourself building? Today, the next people in surah seven, and the next brother sent to them. Day four hundred ten.

In northwest Arabia, near the town of al-Ula, enormous tombs are carved straight into sandstone cliffs, their doorways cut like temple fronts. Muslim tradition has long linked this region, al-Hijr, with the people of Thamud. Archaeologists date the carved tombs standing there now to the Nabataeans, a later people. But the Qur'an says Thamud, too, carved homes out of mountains. And it tells of a sign sent to them that wasn't a wall or a tower at all. It was an animal. A she-camel.
screen: `TOMBS CARVED INTO CLIFFS.` → `AL-HIJR, AND THAMUD.` → `A SIGN THAT WAS AN ANIMAL.`

segments.voice: Verse seventy-three: to Thamud, their brother Salih. Same message as Hud: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then he points to a sign. This is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you. Let her eat in Allah's earth, and don't touch her with harm, or a painful punishment will take you. The Arabic is naqat Allah, the camel of God, and the phrase gives an ordinary animal enormous dignity. Surah twenty-six adds a detail: the water was to be shared, a day for her to drink and a day for the people. The test was almost too simple. Leave her alone. Share the well. That's all. Salih reminds them of their blessings: Allah made them successors after 'Ad, gave them plains to build palaces on and mountains to carve into homes. The proud chiefs mock the poorer people who believed. And then, verse seventy-seven, they hamstring the she-camel and say to Salih, bring on what you threaten. Surah ninety-one says it was done by the most wretched of them, while the people went along. The earthquake took them, and morning found them fallen in their homes. When the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ later passed through al-Hijr on the way to Tabuk, Bukhari reports that he told his companions not to enter the dwellings of those who were punished except in tears. Elsewhere, hadith tell of a man forgiven for giving water to a thirsty dog, and a woman punished for starving a cat. In this tradition, how people treat an animal is never a small thing.
screen: `THEIR BROTHER SALIH.` · `NAQAT ALLAH — THE CAMEL OF GOD.` · `A DAY TO DRINK, A DAY FOR YOU.` · `THEY HAMSTRUNG HER.` · then, large: `LEAVE HER TO GRAZE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Picture an animal you'll likely cross today: a pigeon on the sidewalk, a neighbor's dog, a cat in an alley, a bee at a window. See it going about its business, eating, drinking, resting. Then picture yourself simply letting it be: not chasing, not shooing, not honking, not swatting. Maybe leaving a little water out. Hold that picture of an animal left in peace. The bell holds the time.
Salih. A prophet sent to Thamud, and a sign, a she-camel, that asked only to be left in peace and given her share of water. Today's word.
Your line: leave her to graze. Today, leave one animal in peace, on purpose, and if you can, set out some water. Day four hundred ten.

411.title: Shu'ayb and the scales
411.hook: Shu'ayb tells Madyan to give full measure and not cheat people of their things (7:85)
411.howItsDone: Muslim jurists treat honest weights and measures as a religious duty, and Islamic cities historically had a market inspector, the muhtasib, who checked scales; many Muslim traders cite Shu'ayb and surah eighty-three.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Salih and the she-camel. Your line was leave her to graze. Did an animal get left in peace? Today, the third brother in a row, and this time the problem is in the marketplace. Day four hundred eleven.
screen: `SALIH AND THE SHE-CAMEL — LEAVE HER TO GRAZE.`

segments.voice: A bag of chips that's mostly air. A gas pump that's off by a fraction. An invoice padded with an hour nobody worked. A shop scale that's been nudged so a kilo is a little less than a kilo. Each one is small. Each one is easy to deny. And every one of them adds up, across thousands of customers, to someone getting rich by taking a sliver from everyone. The Qur'an tells of a whole town that ran on slivers, and of the prophet sent to them, Shu'ayb.
screen: `A BAG THAT'S MOSTLY AIR.` → `A SCALE, NUDGED.` → `A TOWN THAT RAN ON SLIVERS.`

segments.voice: Verse eighty-five: to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb. Madyan was a trading people, many place them in northwest Arabia, near the Gulf of Aqaba. Shu'ayb begins with the same call as Hud and Salih: worship Allah, you have no god but Him. Then, in Pickthall's words, he says: “give full measure and full weight and wrong not mankind in their goods.” The word for weight there, mizan, is the balance scale itself. And the phrase translated their goods is ashya'ahum, literally their things: don't shortchange people in anything that's theirs. He adds: don't spread corruption in the land after it has been set right. In the next verse, he warns them about lurking on every road to threaten travelers. The town's leaders answer with an ultimatum: leave, Shu'ayb, you and everyone who believes with you, or come back to our ways. His reply is a short question: even if we hate them? He won't go back, he says, and he asks God to judge between them with truth. Notice what the town is defending. Not only its gods. A way of doing business that worked very well for the people at the top. Some commentators identified Shu'ayb with the father-in-law of Musa; many others disagreed, and the Qur'an doesn't say. The end of Madyan, verse ninety-one, is the earthquake again. But the warning outlived the town. A whole short surah, eighty-three, opens with woe to those who give short measure. Fair weight is not a footnote in this tradition. It sits right next to worship.
screen: `THEIR BROTHER SHU'AYB.` · `MIZAN — THE BALANCE SCALE.` · `LEAVE, OR COME BACK TO OUR WAYS.` · `WOE TO THOSE WHO GIVE SHORT MEASURE.` · then, large: `GIVE FULL MEASURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of your own scales, wherever you measure something out for others: the hours on a timesheet, the change at a register, the effort on a group project, the split of a dinner bill, the slice of cake you cut for someone else. Is there one place where you've been giving a little short? Picture yourself today giving it full, maybe a touch more. Notice how that feels. The bell holds the time.
Shu'ayb. The prophet sent to Madyan, who told a trading town to give full measure and full weight, and wrong no one in their things. Today's word.
Your line: full measure. Today, give fair weight in one thing, your time, your work, your change, a little more than strictly owed. Day four hundred eleven.

412.title: Let me see You
412.hook: Musa asks to see Allah, the mountain crumbles, and he falls fainting, then repents (7:143)
412.carry: the mountain could not bear it
412.howItsDone: Muslims honor Musa as kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to; the scene at the mountain is often recited and taught as a picture of longing for God, and of His majesty beyond what creation can bear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shu'ayb and the scales. Your line was full measure. Where did you give a little more than owed? Today surah seven reaches Musa, and a request nobody expects. Day four hundred twelve.

Musa has been called from beside a fire, has stood before Pharaoh, has watched the sea split. Now Allah sets him an appointment: thirty nights on the mountain, completed with ten more, forty in all. He goes up alone. And there, Allah speaks to him. That's why Muslims give Musa the title kalimullah, the one Allah spoke to. That might seem like enough. Musa, standing in that conversation, asks for one thing more.
screen: `FORTY NIGHTS ON THE MOUNTAIN.` → `KALIMULLAH — THE ONE ALLAH SPOKE TO.` → `ONE THING MORE.`

segments.voice: Verse one-forty-three. Musa says: rabbi arini anzur ilayk. My Lord, show me, so that I may look at You. It's a request made out of longing, not arrogance. And the answer comes, in Pickthall's words: “Thou wilt not see Me, but gaze upon the mountain!” If it stays firm in its place, then you will see Me. Then Allah reveals His glory to the mountain, and the mountain is crushed, made level, turned to dust. And Musa falls down unconscious. When he comes to, his first words are: glory be to You. I turn to You in repentance, and I am the first of the believers. Notice what he repents of. Some commentators say it wasn't a sin, exactly, but asking for more than a human being can bear. The text doesn't scold the longing. It shows its size by showing a mountain that couldn't hold it. Jews and Christians know a related scene in Exodus, where Moses asks to see God's glory and is told no one can see God's face and live. Each tradition tells it in its own way. And the swoon at the mountain echoes later. A hadith in Bukhari says that on the Day of Resurrection, when people fall unconscious, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ will be the first to wake, and he'll find Musa already there, holding the side of the Throne. The Prophet said he didn't know whether Musa woke first, or was spared that swoon because of the one he'd already had on the mountain. Musa's longing, it seems, wasn't wasted.
screen: `MY LORD, SHOW ME.` · `LOOK AT THE MOUNTAIN.` · `CRUSHED TO DUST; MUSA FALLS.` · `GLORY TO YOU; I TURN TO YOU.` · then, large: `THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: If you can, go stand under something vast: a big sky, a tall tree, a building that makes you tip your head back, even a ceiling in a large room. If you can't move, picture one. Look up. Notice your size next to it. Then remember the mountain in the story, far larger than you, unable to bear a glimpse of the glory. Let the smallness feel safe, not crushing. The bell holds the time.
Arini, show me. Musa's request on the mountain, answered with a crumbling peak, a swoon, and glory to You. Today's word.
Your line: the mountain could not bear it. Today, when something makes you feel small, let it bring back the mountain, and the longing that climbed it. Day four hundred twelve.

413.title: "Am I not your Lord?"
413.hook: the souls of Adam's children are asked, am I not your Lord, and say, yes (7:172)
413.howItsDone: Muslims teach 7:172 as the primordial covenant (al-mithaq) and link it to the fitrah, the natural disposition toward God; Sufi poets, especially in Persian, call it the day of Alast.

segments.voice: Yesterday: arini, let me see You, and the mountain. Your line was the mountain could not bear it. A week ends today: no waste, a quiet du'a, Hud, Salih, Shu'ayb, Musa on the mountain. Now a question older than all of them. Day four hundred thirteen.
screen: `ARINI — THE MOUNTAIN COULD NOT BEAR IT.`

segments.voice: A song heard for the first time that seems already known. A street never walked before that somehow says, I know this. Persian poets had a name for an older version of that: the day of Alast. They meant a moment before anyone was born, when every human soul heard a single question and gave a single answer. They took it from one verse in surah seven. And the word Alast is simply the first word of that question in Arabic.
screen: `A SONG YOU'VE ALWAYS KNOWN.` → `THE DAY OF ALAST.` → `ONE QUESTION, ONE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Verse one-seventy-two says that your Lord brought out from the children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify about themselves. Then the question, in Pickthall's words: “Am I not your Lord? They said: Yea, verily. We testify.” In Arabic: alastu bi-rabbikum? Qalu bala. Am I not your Lord? They said, yes. The verse gives the reason: so that no one can say on the Day of Resurrection, we didn't know about this. Scholars call this al-mithaq, the covenant. The word comes from a root meaning to bind firmly, like a rope tied tight, and it appears in the verses just before this one. What exactly happened? Muslim scholars have read it in two main ways. Some, citing a hadith in which Umar asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ about this verse, take it as a real event: every soul, drawn out and asked, before the world began. Others read it as a picture of human nature itself, the fitrah: that every person is made with the knowledge of their Lord built in, and the testimony is written into who they are. Both readings agree on the most striking part. In this telling, faith isn't something foreign that's added later. It's remembering. Sufi poets took this up. Rumi wrote of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, crying out to go home. Some readers hear in that the soul longing for the day it said yes. The Qur'an's own word for the answer is tiny: bala. Yes.
screen: `ALASTU BI-RABBIKUM?` · `QALU BALA — THEY SAID, YES.` · `AN EVENT, OR HUMAN NATURE?` · `FAITH AS REMEMBERING.` · then, large: `WE SAID YES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow down. Imagine, just for a moment, that before your first breath you were asked a question, and you answered. You don't have to decide what you believe about it. Just sit inside the picture. Then, if it fits for you, on one quiet out-breath, let the word bala, yes, pass through your mind. If it doesn't fit, simply notice what in you wants to say yes to something larger. The bell holds the time.
Mithaq. The covenant: the firm pledge of 7:172, when the children of Adam were asked, am I not your Lord, and said, yes. Today's word.
Your line: we said yes. Today, when something feels strangely familiar, a sky, a kindness, a line of the Qur'an, let it be a small remembering. Day four hundred thirteen.

what it means: the covenant of Alast: every person, in this telling, once said yes to their Lord, so faith is a remembering.
what a scholar hears: bala, not na'am, answers a negative question affirmatively; the hadith of Umar (Muwatta, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi) supports the literal reading, while others read 7:172 as fitrah.
